details: Atmospheric aerosol size classification: Ultrafine: <0.1 µm; Fine: 0.1-2.5 µm (PM2.5); Coarse: 2.5-10 µm (PM10); Giant: >10 µm; Chernobyl release produced aerosols in multiple size ranges: (1) Volatile condensation aerosols (Cs; I; Te): formed as vapor from overheated fuel condensed at distance; AMAD 0.1-1 µm (fine fraction = respirable = alveolar deposition); long atmospheric residence time (hours-days); traveled thousands of km; (2) Fuel particles: 4-150 µm (coarse to giant); deposited near NPP (<10km); not respirable (nasal/pharyngeal deposition); (3) Graphite particles: 1-100 µm; deposited within 1-30km; (4) Steam explosion fragmented fuel: wide size distribution
chernobyl_application: AMAD (Activity Median Aerodynamic Diameter): 50% of total activity in particles smaller than AMAD; 50% larger; key parameter for lung dosimetry (determines deposition fraction in different respiratory tract regions); Chernobyl Cs-137 AMAD (measured at distance 100-2000km): 0.3-2 µm = primarily fine mode condensation aerosol; deposited in alveoli if inhaled (highest lung dose); Cs-137 aerosol = CsOH/Cs₂SO₄ condensed on background aerosol surface; at 3km NW of NPP: fuel particles dominate (4-150 µm); much less lung deposition; external gamma from ground deposition more important near NPP; inhalation more important far from NPP (volatile aerosols dominate)

details: Dry deposition velocity V_d: rate of aerosol deposition to surface without precipitation; V_d = deposition flux / air concentration (m/s); strongly size-dependent: <0.1 µm particles: Brownian diffusion dominant; V_d ~0.001-0.01 mm/s; 0.1-1 µm (fine): lowest V_d (minimum 0.1-1 mm/s; aerosol 'Greenfield gap'); >1 µm: increasing gravitational settling; 10 µm: V_d ~10-50 mm/s; specific radionuclide V_d: I₂ (gaseous): 10-50 mm/s (reactive gas; very high); CH₃I (organic iodine): 0.01-0.1 mm/s; Cs-137 CsOH aerosol: 1-3 mm/s; Pu fuel particle (50 µm): ~50+ mm/s (rapid near-field deposition)
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl deposition physics: 1% dry vs 99% wet: most Cs-137 (volatile fine aerosol) deposited via wet deposition (rainfall interception); 99% of Cs-137 deposition in areas with rain during plume passage; areas with no rain: only dry deposition (1% contribution); explains spatial heterogeneity: single thunderstorm May 8 1986 deposited essentially all Cs-137 that reached Bavaria/Austria in one event; areas that had clear skies as plume passed: very low deposition; monitoring data: May 8 Bavaria rain event = 10,000-100,000 Bq/m² Cs-137 vs <1000 Bq/m² in equivalent-distance areas with no rain during plume passage

details: Wet deposition scavenging: below-cloud scavenging coefficient Λ (s⁻¹) = rate of aerosol removal by rainfall per unit time; Λ = S × V_t / v_drop where S = collection efficiency; V_t = rain terminal velocity; v_drop = drop volume; empirical: Λ = 2×10⁻⁵ × R^0.82 (s⁻¹) where R = rainfall rate (mm/hr); at R = 5 mm/hr: Λ = 5.7×10⁻⁵ s⁻¹ → effective aerosol half-life in column = ln2/5.7×10⁻⁵ = 12,000s = 3.3 hr; in-cloud scavenging (nucleation + impaction within cloud): 10-100× more efficient than below-cloud; washout ratio W = (Bq/g water) / (Bq/g air) = typically 10⁵-10⁶ for soluble particles; CsOH = highly water-soluble → W near upper limit → efficiently washed out
chernobyl_application: 'Hotspot' formation mechanism: radioactive cloud passes over region; no rain = minimal deposition; cloud reaches area with convective storm; rainfall begins; soluble Cs-137 aerosol efficiently scavenged → 1-10 hours of rain deposits entire column inventory; spots of 10-100× higher contamination than surrounding areas = hotspots; examples: Gomel Belarus (rain during peak plume); Lugano Switzerland (Alpine thunderstorm May 2); Bayern Germany (May 8 rain); Red Forest immediate area (rain April 26-27 + close proximity + high concentration); Cs-137 hotspot formation = meteorological accident within radiological accident; explains why some areas 500km away have higher contamination than some areas 100km away

details: Pasquill-Gifford (PG) stability classes for atmospheric diffusion: Class A: very unstable (strong insolation; wind <2 m/s); σ_y and σ_z largest; rapid dispersion; Class B: unstable; Class C: slightly unstable; Class D: neutral (overcast or wind >6 m/s; most common); Class E: slightly stable (light winds; evening); Class F: stable (calm clear night; inversions); Briggs sigma formulas (per class): σ_y = ax (Class D: a=0.16); σ_z = bx^c (Class D: b=0.12; c=0.9); σ determined at downwind distance x (km); Gaussian plume concentration: C(x,y,z) = Q/(2πσ_yσ_z·u) × exp(-y²/2σ_y²) × [exp(-(z-h)²/2σ_z²) + exp(-(z+h)²/2σ_z²)]
chernobyl_application: Conditions April 26-27 1986: clear sky; calm winds (2-3 m/s); night transitioning to day; stability: Class D (neutral) to Class F (stable) depending on time; conditions were: conducive to limited dispersion at ground level but efficient vertical transport of hot plume; plume rise: ~1200m effective plume height (thermal buoyancy from burning graphite + steam) → most activity lofted above mixing layer → transported far with minimal near-ground concentration; 'good' meteorological conditions from dispersion standpoint at Pripyat (diluted at Pripyat due to plume height) but 'bad' from international transport (lofted plume traveled to Scandinavia); atmospheric_dispersion_parameters_REAL.csv has full Briggs formulae

details: Resuspension factor K_p: ratio of airborne concentration (Bq/m³) to surface contamination (Bq/m²); K_p = C_air / A_surface (units: m⁻¹); range: K_p = 10⁻⁹ to 10⁻⁵ m⁻¹; fresh contamination (1986): K_p ≈ 10⁻⁵ m⁻¹ (high; aerosol loosely bound to surface); aged contamination (2026): K_p ≈ 10⁻⁹ to 10⁻⁸ m⁻¹ (low; Cs-137 fixed in FES clay); K_p decreases with time (aging = fixation); wildfire increases K_p by 2-4 orders magnitude (disturbs fixation; combustion aerosols carry Cs-137); vehicle traffic in CEZ: increases K_p locally by 1-2 orders magnitude (2022 Russian military vehicles driving on soil raised dose rates 70×); factor ~10-100 increase from vehicle disturbance vs 2-4 orders from fire
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl 2026 resuspension: aged soil Cs-137 K_p ≈ 10⁻⁹ m⁻¹; surface contamination 100,000 Bq/m²; airborne Cs-137 = 10⁻⁹ × 10⁵ = 10⁻⁴ Bq/m³ = 0.0001 Bq/m³; current CEZ air monitoring: ~0.001-0.01 Bq/m³ (dominated by soil disturbance + background weapons fallout resuspension); occupational limit for Cs-137 in air: 20,000 Bq/m³; CEZ levels: 10⁶-10⁸ × below limit; wildfire 2020: K_p temporarily ~10⁻⁷ → air Cs-137 100 Bq/m³ peak during fire → 200× normal but still well below occupational limit; explains why wildfire ecological/monitoring concern >> occupational concern

details: Gravitational settling velocity (Stokes regime): v_s = 2r²(ρ_particle - ρ_air)g / (9η); where r = particle radius (m); ρ_particle = 2500 kg/m³ (typical mineral aerosol); ρ_air = 1.2 kg/m³; g = 9.81 m/s²; η = 1.81×10⁻⁵ Pa·s (air at 20°C); for r = 10 µm: v_s = 2×(10⁻⁵)²×2500×9.81/(9×1.81×10⁻⁵) = 0.030 m/s = 30 mm/s (gravitational settling dominates); r = 1 µm: v_s = 0.0003 m/s = 0.3 mm/s (Brownian diffusion comparable); r = 0.1 µm: v_s = 3×10⁻⁶ m/s (diffusion dominates); Stokes valid for particles < ~30 µm (Re << 1)
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl fuel particle settling: Pu fuel particles 50-150 µm; v_s at 50 µm: 0.007 m/s; atmospheric transit at 3 m/s wind: horizontal range = 3/0.007 × (plume height) = 430 × 1200m = 516 km maximum theoretical; actual: fuel particles (dense UO₂ = 10,970 kg/m³): v_s at 50 µm = 2×(25×10⁻⁶)²×10,970×9.81/(9×1.81×10⁻⁵) = 0.82 m/s = 820 mm/s; range at 3 m/s wind and 1200m plume: 3/0.82 × 1200 = 4,400m = 4.4 km; explains why fuel particles concentrate within 10km of NPP; lighter condensation aerosols (Cs-137; density ~2000 kg/m³; r=0.3µm): v_s << 0.001 m/s → gravitational settling negligible → transported thousands of km

details: Turbulent diffusion (K-theory): atmospheric transport = mean wind advection + turbulent diffusion; K-theory: flux J = -K × dC/dx where K = eddy diffusivity (m²/s); K_horizontal = 10²-10⁵ m²/s (varies with scale; Richardson's K ~ L^(4/3) cascade); K_vertical = 0.1-100 m²/s (strongly stability-dependent); Class A (unstable): K_z = 100 m²/s; Class F (stable night): K_z = 0.1-1 m²/s; Chernobyl plume vs K-theory: near-field (< 100km): Gaussian plume model good approximation; far-field (> 100km): Lagrangian particle tracking (HYSPLIT; FLEXPART) more appropriate; mesoscale: ERA5 reanalysis wind fields; synoptic: 100-1000km; global: CTBTO global transport model
chernobyl_application: Turbulent diffusion and dose: dilution factor: at distance x downwind (Class D conditions): σ_y = 0.16x; σ_z = 0.12x^0.9; C ∝ 1/(σ_y σ_z) ∝ 1/x^1.9 (roughly inverse-square for Class D); chi/Q (dispersion factor) at 1km Class D: ~1-3×10⁻⁴ s/m³; at 10km: ~10⁻⁶ s/m³; at 100km: ~10⁻⁸ s/m³; factor 100 dilution per 10× distance; HOWEVER: Chernobyl plume was NOT simple Gaussian (intermittent source; graphite fire; varied meteorology over 14 days); transport model accuracy ±30-50% for complex multi-phase release; better than order-of-magnitude for dose reconstruction purposes
